en: Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya, Volume One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

1. The Section on the General Presentation of the Essential Framework. First, within the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra*, prior to the Bhagavat, a Bodhisattva who has already attained skillful entry into the Mahāyāna spoke in order to reveal the greatness of the essence (*svabhāva*) of the Mahāyāna.
That is to say, based on the Mahāyāna, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of preeminent and supreme teachings:
first, the preeminent and supreme teaching on the basis of the known;
second, the preeminent and supreme teaching on the characteristics of the known; [and so forth].
Third, the discourse on the excellence of the entry into the characteristics of the knowable;
fourth, the discourse on the excellence of the causes and results of that entry;
fifth, the discourse on the excellence of the distinctions in the cultivation of those causes and results.
Sixth, the discourse on the excellence and preeminence of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) within these very distinctions of cultivation;
seventh, the discourse on the excellence and preeminence of higher mental training (*adhicitta*) therein;
eighth, the discourse on the excellence and preeminence of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) therein.
Ninth, the discourse on the excellence of the abandonment of those fruits;
tenth, the discourse on the excellence of the wisdom of those fruits.
By these various phrases from the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, it is revealed that the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha.
Furthermore, how is it made manifest?

It is because these ten points, as here explained, have never been taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle, but are seen taught everywhere within the Mahāyāna; namely, the ālayavijñāna, which is designated as the essence of the basis of the knowable (*jñeyāśraya*).

The three natures—first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—are designated as the essence of the characteristics of the knowable.
The nature of consciousness-only is called the essence of entering the characteristics of the knowable.
The six perfections are called the essence of the cause and fruit of that entry.
The ten stages of the bodhisattva are called the essence of the distinctions in the cultivation of that cause and fruit.
The bodhisattva vows are designated here as the essence of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
The *Śūraṅgama*, *Gaganagañja*, and other such samādhis are designated here as the essence of higher mental cultivation (*adhicitta*).
Non-conceptual wisdom is designated here as the essence of superior insight (*adhiprajñā*).
Non-abiding nirvana is designated as the essence of its fruit, which is abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
The three bodies of the Buddha (*trikāya*):

First, the *svābhāvika-kāya* (essential body); second, the *sambhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body); and third, the *nairmāṇika-kāya* (emanation body)—these are designated as the essence of the wisdom that is their fruit.
By means of these ten points thus explained, it is shown that the Mahāyāna differs from the Śrāvakayāna;
furthermore, it is shown to be supreme, for the Blessed One taught them solely for the sake of bodhisattvas.
Therefore, one should know that it is solely by relying on the Mahāyāna that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of superior and most excellent speech.

Furthermore, how is it that through these ten kinds of superior and most excellent Tathāgata speech, the Mahāyāna is revealed as truly being the word of the Buddha, while the Śrāvaka vehicle is excluded from having the nature of the Mahāyāna?
These ten points have never been taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle, but are seen taught everywhere within the Mahāyāna.
That is to say, these ten points are most capable of inducing the nature of great enlightenment;
they are well-established.
It is compliant and non-contradictory;
it serves as the means for realizing the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Regarding this, there are two verses:
“The basis of the knowable and the characteristics of the knowable, Its entry, its cause and fruit, its distinct cultivations, the three trainings,
Its fruits of abandonment and gnosis— Subsumed within the Supreme Vehicle, these are the excellences.”
"This explains what is seen here and what is not seen elsewhere;
because this is the most excellent cause for awakening, the Mahāyāna is accepted as the true word of the Buddha, being superior due to its exposition of the ten topics."
Furthermore, why are these ten bases taught in this specific sequence?
It is because Bodhisattvas must first become proficient in the causes of all phenomena before they can attain skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Thereafter, regarding all phenomena produced from conditions, one should become skilled in their characteristics, for this enables one to effectively distance oneself from the two extremes of the errors of superimposition and denial.

Thereafter, having thus cultivated skill, the bodhisattva should correctly penetrate and become proficient in the characteristics of the apprehended object, thereby causing the mind to be liberated from all hindrances.

Subsequently, having attained mastery over the characteristics of the objects of knowledge, the six perfections practiced during the preceding stage of application should be further perfected through their realization, so that the superior intention may become purified.

Thereafter, one should diligently cultivate the six pāramitās, which are embraced by the pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*), according to their specific distinctions throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);
that is to say, this must be accomplished over the course of three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Thereafter, one should bring to completion the trainings of the three bodhisattvas.
Once these are perfected, one should manifest the realization of their fruits: nirvāṇa and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, the ten topics are taught in this specific sequence.
Furthermore, within this exposition, all Mahāyāna teachings reach their ultimate conclusion.
Section Two: The Basis of the Knowable (*Jñeyāśraya-bhāga*). In this section, first of all, the basis of the knowable is explained; that is, the *ālayavijñāna*.
In what place did the Blessed One speak of the *ālayavijñāna* by the name of *ālayavijñāna*?
It is said that the Bhagavat spoke in a verse within the *Abhidharmamahāyānasūtra*:
“The element from beginningless time, The common support of all phenomena, ... [as cited in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*]"
"From this arise the various realms of existence, as well as the realization of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, regarding this very point, a verse is spoken:
"Because it contains all phenomena, the consciousness of all seeds—"
"Therefore it is named Ālaya; this I have revealed for the sake of the Victorious Ones.
Thus, for now, I have cited the Āgama as proof.
Furthermore, for what reason is this consciousness called the *ālayavijñāna*?
Because all phenomena belonging to the category of defiled existence are stored within this [consciousness] as its fruit-nature,
and because this very consciousness is stored within them as their cause-nature,
it is therefore called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Because sentient beings grasp and conceal this consciousness as a self, it is therefore called the *ālayavijñāna*.
Furthermore, this consciousness is also named the *ādānavijñāna*.
Regarding the *Āgama* herein, as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*:
“The appropriating consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*) is profound and subtle;
Containing all seeds like a torrential stream, I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, Lest they conceptualize and grasp it as a self.”
For what reason is this consciousness also called the *ādāna-vijñāna*?
Because it appropriates all material sense-faculties and because it is the basis for the appropriation of all personal existences.
Why is this so? Because the material sense faculties are sustained by this [appropriation], they do not perish but persist throughout one's lifespan.
Furthermore, at the moment of linking rebirth within the continuum, it takes up that birth and thereby appropriates the physical body.
For this reason, this consciousness is also called the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
It is also called "mind" (*citta*), as the Blessed One said:
"Mind, mentation, and consciousness—these three."
In this context, there are two types of intention:

first, it serves as the basis for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); that is, the consciousness that has just ceased can serve as the generative basis for the mental consciousness.
Second, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is always associated with four afflictions:
first, the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*); third, self-love (*ātmasneha*); and fourth, ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is the basis for the defilement of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, consciousness arises from that first basis;

it is the second [basis], defilement, because its meaning is the discernment of objects, because of the meaning of "immediately preceding," and because of the meaning of "cogitation"; thus, *manas* (mind) constitutes two types.
Furthermore, how is it known that there exists a defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*)?
It is because if this did not exist, the non-common ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*) could not exist, which would result in a logical fallacy.
Furthermore, the five types of similar phenomena (*pañca-sabhāga*) cannot exist either, as this would result in logical fallacies.
Why is this? Because the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) must necessarily have simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*), such as the eyes and so forth.
Furthermore, the etymological derivation [of the term] would also be untenable, as it would result in a logical fallacy.

Moreover, there would be no distinction between the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), which would likewise result in a logical fallacy.
That is to say, the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is manifested by the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), whereas the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is not;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between these two types of attainments.

Furthermore, during the course of a single lifetime in the Heaven of No-Perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), there would be the fault of there being no affliction, because within that state there would be neither grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) nor the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Furthermore, because the activity of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is perceptible at all times— namely, within minds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral— if this were not the case,
then only in unwholesome minds would the afflictions of "I" and "mine" manifest in association with it, rather than in wholesome or neutral states.
Therefore, if one posits that they function as co-existent [factors] rather than functioning as associated [factors], this fault does not arise.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"If it were non-common ignorance, And shared the same nature as the five [aggregates],"
Regarding the exegesis, there are two distinct points: if [the self] did not exist, both would result in fallacies;
there would be no birth in the realm of non-conception, and the persistence of the grasping for a self would become a fallacy;
furthermore, the grasping for a self would never cease to follow one, nor would it exist in any way whatsoever.
If the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) did not exist, there would be a contradiction regarding the [simultaneous] occurrence of two or three [minds];
without it, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) would not be possible in any situation.
It constantly acts as an obstacle to the arising of the mind directed toward true reality (*tattvārtha-citta*).
"Coexisting with all factors; this refers to the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Because its nature is defiled, it is of the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) category and is always associated with the four afflictions.

Just as the afflictions of the two entanglements—those of the form and formless realms—are subsumed under the nature of obscured-neutral, because the entanglements of the form and formless realms are concealed by śamatha;
this [manas] likewise follows [the object] subtly at all times.
Regarding the third [aspect], the essence of mind: apart from the ālayavijñāna, no other [essence] can be found.
Therefore, it is established that the ālayavijñāna constitutes the essence of mind; with this as its seed, the manas and the [six] consciousnesses evolve.
For what reason is it also called "mind" (*citta*)?
Because it is accumulated by the seeds perfumed by various phenomena (*dharma*).
Furthermore, why is this mind not called the *ālayavijñāna* or the *ādānavijñāna* within the Śrāvaka vehicle?
Because it is subsumed within this profound and subtle object. Why is this so?

Because the Śrāvakas do not operate within the sphere of knowledge regarding all objects; therefore, even without this teaching, their wisdom is established and their liberation is accomplished. For this reason, it was not taught to them.
If bodhisattvas are certain to engage with all objects and states of knowledge, it is for this reason that [this teaching] is expounded.
Apart from this wisdom, it is not easy to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Furthermore, within the Śrāvakayāna, the ālayavijñāna has also been taught through a different method and with intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), as stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
"Worldly beings love the ālaya, delight in the ālaya, rejoice in the ālaya, and find pleasure in the ālaya;

for the sake of abandoning such an ālaya, when the True Dharma is preached, they listen attentively with reverence, abide with a mind seeking understanding, and practice in accordance with the Dharma."
"The appearance in the world of the Tathāgata, and likewise the emergence in the world of such a most marvelous and rare true Dharma"—
it is through this intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) in the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-caturguṇa-sūtra* of the Śrāvaka vehicle that the ālayavijñāna has already been revealed.
In the Āgamas of the Mahāsāṃghika school, this is also taught under a different designation with intentional meaning as the *mūlavijñāna* (root-consciousness), just as a tree depends upon its roots.
Within the Mahīśāsaka school, it is also taught under a different designation with intentional meaning as the *ātyantika-saṃsāra-skandha* (the aggregates that persist until the end of saṃsāra).
In certain places and at certain times, one may observe the cessation of form and mind; however, within the *ālayavijñāna*, those seeds do not undergo cessation.

Thus, the *ālaya*—the basis of all that is to be known—is described as having the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*, the nature of the *ādānavijñāna*, the nature of the *citta*, the nature of the *ālaya*, the nature of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and the nature of the aggregates that persist until the end of saṃsāra.
Through these various designations, the *ālayavijñāna* becomes the great royal road.
Furthermore, there is another class [of thinkers] who claim that *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* have the same meaning despite different names.
This position is untenable; since distinct meanings can be discerned between *manas* and *vijñāna*, one should know that the meaning of *citta* must likewise differ [from them].

Furthermore, there is another class [of people] who say: "Regarding what the Bhagavat has taught—that sentient beings are attached to the *ālaya*, and so forth, as explained at length—in this context, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are designated by the name *ālaya*."
Others again claim that the sensation of pleasure associated with craving is the *ālaya*.
Still others claim that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the *ālaya*.
These various teachers, being ignorant of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) due to their reliance on scripture and personal realization, hold such views.
Establishing the name *ālaya* in this manner is also inconsistent with the principles established according to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
However, for those who are not deluded, if they take this storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and establish it as being called *ālaya*, such an establishment is the most excellent.
What is meant by "most excellent"?

If the five aggregates of clinging were called the *ālaya*, it would be illogical for them to be designated as such, because when one is born into the miserable destinies—a realm of exclusively suffering that is utterly loathsome—sentient beings never give rise to any affection or delight toward it; therefore, it is unreasonable for them to grasp and store [the seeds] therein, since they constantly seek to abandon it as quickly as possible.

If the sensation of pleasure associated with craving were called the *ālayavijñāna*, it would not exist from the fourth dhyāna upward; furthermore, sentient beings possessing those states would constantly feel aversion toward it, and thus it would be illogical for them to harbor [the seeds] within it.

If the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) were called the *ālaya*, then those who have faith and understanding in this true Dharma regarding selflessness would always feel aversion toward it; thus, it would be illogical for it to be that which is grasped and stored within as the *ālaya*.

The ālayavijñāna is comprised within the nature of an internal self; thus, even when one is born in the miserable realms where there is constant suffering and seeks to escape the aggregates of suffering, one remains bound by the attachment to the ālaya as a self and never seeks to abandon it.

Although those born in the fourth dhyāna or above always feel aversion toward the pleasure associated with craving, they remain bound by the love of self toward the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Likewise, although those who have faith and understanding in this True Dharma and loathe the view of a self, they remain bound by the love of self toward the storehouse consciousness.
Therefore, establishing the name *ālayavijñāna* as "the storehouse" (*ālaya*) is most excellent.
Thus, having explained the various designations for the establishment of the *ālayavijñāna*, how is its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) to be understood?
The establishment of these characteristics is briefly of three kinds:
first, the establishment of specific characteristics; second, the establishment of causal characteristics; and third, the establishment of resultant characteristics.

Regarding the establishment of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the ālayavijñāna herein: it refers to its being the cause for the arising of all phenomena belonging to the category of defilement (*saṃkleśapakṣa*), by virtue of its capacity to maintain the corresponding seeds (*bīja*).

Regarding the establishment of the causal characteristic (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*) of the ālayavijñāna herein: it refers to this very ālayavijñāna, which consists of all seeds, acting at all times as the cause for the manifestation of those phenomena belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa-pakṣya*).

Regarding the establishment of the resultant characteristic (*phalalakṣaṇa*) of the ālayavijñāna herein: it refers to the fact that the ālayavijñāna arises in continuous succession based precisely upon the latencies (*vāsanā*) of all those factors belonging to the category of defilement (*saṃkleśapakṣadharma*) that have existed from beginningless time.
Furthermore, what is called "perfuming" (vāsanā)?
Perfuming is that which expresses.
What is it that is expressed?
This means that based on those phenomena, there arises and ceases simultaneously with them a causal nature capable of producing them; this is what is signified.

It is like the perfuming of sesame seeds by flowers: the sesame seeds and the flowers arise and cease together, and these sesame seeds are produced bearing the causal factor capable of generating that fragrance.

Furthermore, as for those established as practitioners characterized by greed and so forth, the latencies of greed and so forth arise and perish simultaneously with that greed; this mind arises bearing the causes for its own production.

Alternatively, one who is "learned" (bahuśruta) is so called because of the perfuming of extensive learning; this mind arises and perishes simultaneously with the mental attention based on what has been heard, and it arises bearing the causal seeds of that [learning]. Because it is able to maintain these perfumings, such a person is named a "holder of the Dharma."
The principle of the perfuming of the ālayavijñāna should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, do the seeds of the various defiled phenomena within the ālayavijñāna abide as distinct entities?
Are they not distinct?
It is not that there exists some separate, substantial entity as a seed residing within this [consciousness], nor is it the case that they are not different.
Rather, the ālayavijñāna arises in such a way that it possesses specific functional capacities capable of producing those [phenomena]; this is called the "all-seed consciousness."
Furthermore, how can it be seen that the ālayavijñāna and those various defiled phenomena act as mutual causes for one another simultaneously?
It is like a bright lamp, where the flame and the wick arise and burn simultaneously, acting as mutual causes for one another.
Furthermore, just as bundles of reeds support one another so that they do not fall simultaneously,
one should observe that the principle of mutual causality here is likewise.

Just as the ālayavijñāna is the cause of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), and all defiled phenomena are also the cause of the ālayavijñāna, it is solely on this basis that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is established, for no other causal conditions can be found.
How can perfuming (*vāsanā*), which is itself without difference or mixture, serve as the cause for those phenomena that possess difference and mixture?

It is like a cloth dyed with various coloring agents: at the time of dyeing, although no distinct, mixed, or multi-variegated categories are yet perceptible, once it has entered the dye-vat, thereupon upon the cloth there appear variegated, mixed, and multi-variegated patterns of interwoven colors.

The ālayavijñāna is also like this: it is perfumed by diverse and heterogeneous perfuming agents; although at the time of perfuming no such diversity can yet be found, once the fruit—the vessel of defilement—has manifested, there then appear immeasurable categories of diverse and heterogeneous phenomena.
Such dependent origination is extremely subtle and profound within the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, to speak briefly, there are two types of dependent origination:
first, the dependent origination of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); second, the dependent origination of the imagined [distinction between] the agreeable and the disagreeable.

Among these, the arising of all phenomena based upon the ālayavijñāna is called the dependent origination of the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva-pratītyasamutpāda*), because it functions as the causal condition by means of discriminating various intrinsic natures.

Furthermore, there is the twelve-linked dependent origination, which is called the "discriminating dependent origination of the agreeable and the disagreeable," because it serves as the causal nature for discriminating between various agreeable and disagreeable personal existences within the happy and miserable realms.

Within the ālayavijñāna, regarding the first dependent origination, some are deluded by conceptualizing self-nature as the cause, some conceptualize past karma as the cause, some conceptualize the transformations of Īśvara as the cause, some conceptualize a real self as the cause, and some conceptualize it as being without cause or condition.
If one is deluded regarding the second dependent origination, one further discriminates, thinking, "I am the agent" and "I am the experiencer.
It is like a group of many blind men who have never seen an elephant, and someone else explains and demonstrates it to them by means of the elephant.
Among those born blind, some touched the elephant’s trunk, some touched its tusks, some touched its ears, some touched its feet, some touched its tail, and some touched its backbone.
When people asked, "What is the appearance of an elephant?

some said it was like the handle of a plow; some said it was like a pestle; some said it was like a winnowing basket; some said it was like a mortar; some said it was like a broom; and others said that an elephant was like a rocky mountain.

If one does not understand these two types of dependent origination, ignorance is likewise like being born blind. Some conceive of inherent nature (*svabhāva*) as the cause; some conceive of past actions (*pūrvakṛta*) as the cause; some conceive of a sovereign lord (*īśvara*) as the cause; some conceive of a real self (*ātman*) as the cause;
and some conceive of there being neither cause nor condition. Others conceive of a self as the agent and a self as the experiencer.
The nature of the ālayavijñāna—its causal nature, its resultant nature, and so forth—is like one who does not understand the nature of an elephant.

To speak briefly, the ālayavijñāna has as its intrinsic nature the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) with all seeds; it is capable of encompassing the entire self-substance of the three realms and all destinies (gati), and so on.
Regarding this, there are five verses:
"External, internal,
and indistinct."
Regarding these two— namely, the conventional and the ultimate—
it should be known that there are six kinds of seeds:
momentary destruction, coexistence, and it should be known that they constantly follow and evolve.
Determined, dependent on various conditions, capable only of projecting its own fruit,
stable, indeterminate, susceptible to perfuming, and associated with that which perfumes—
what is perfumed is not other than this; such is the characteristic of perfuming.
The six consciousnesses lack association; they contradict one another in three ways of differentiation, and two moments do not coexist.
By these analogies, other [theories] are shown to be fallacious.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are external and internal seeds, which function as the producers and the sustainers.
"Because withering and death arise from what is capable of inducing [a result], and because they perish spontaneously later.
To clarify that internal seeds are not like external seeds, two further verses are spoken:
"One should know that external [seeds] may lack perfuming, whereas internal seeds are not [like this]."
Without the perfuming of hearing and so forth, the arising of the fruit is not logical;
because of the faults of losing what was done and gaining what was not done, it would result in contradiction.
External seeds serve as conditions for the internal, by depending upon that perfuming.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the remaining evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), throughout all personal existences and realms of rebirth, are designated as the "experiencer. As stated in a verse in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*:
"The first is called the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*); The second is named the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*).
Within this [second], there are the mental factors (*caitta*) of experiencing, discriminating, and deliberating."
In this way, these two consciousnesses serve as mutual conditions for one another. As stated in a verse in the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra*:
"All phenomena reside within the storehouse of consciousness, and consciousness likewise resides within all phenomena;
they are mutually the nature of effects, and also eternally the nature of causes."
If, within the first dependent origination, these two consciousnesses serve as mutual causes and conditions, what kind of condition do they constitute within the second dependent origination?
They constitute a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
How many conditions give rise to these six consciousnesses?
They arise from the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Thus, there are these three types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
That is to say, throughout the cycle of birth and death, there are the realms of the desirable and the undesirable, as well as that which experiences them;
these possess four conditions.

Having thus established the various synonyms and characteristics of the ālayavijñāna, how is it known that such synonyms and such characteristics definitively belong only to the ālayavijñāna and not to the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)?
If one were to distance oneself from such an established presentation of the *ālayavijñāna*, neither defilement nor purification could be established:
that is to say, because the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*) would all fail to be established;
and because mundane purification as well as supramundane purification would likewise fail to be established.
Why is it that the defilement of afflictions is not established?
Because it is illogical for the substance of those seeds—produced by the perfuming of the primary afflictions and secondary afflictions—to exist within the six groups of consciousness.

Why is this so? If it is established that visual consciousness arises and ceases simultaneously with afflictions such as greed and their secondary afflictions, then the seeds must be formed by the perfuming of those [afflictions], and not by anything else.

However, if this visual consciousness has already ceased and been interrupted by other consciousnesses, then neither such perfuming nor the basis for that perfuming can be found. It is therefore illogical for a visual consciousness—which lacks a present substantial entity because it has previously ceased and been interrupted by other consciousnesses—to arise simultaneously with those [afflictions] like greed, since that [past consciousness] currently lacks a substantial entity.
It is not logical that a maturation fruit could arise from an action that has no substance in the present, as it did in the past.
Furthermore, the latencies (vāsanā) co-arising with this visual consciousness—such as craving and so forth—are also not established;
for these latencies do not reside within the craving itself, because that craving is the dependent and is not stable.

Nor can it abide within the remaining consciousnesses, because the bases (*āśraya*) of those various consciousnesses are distinct, and furthermore, because there is no certainty regarding their simultaneous arising and ceasing.
Nor can it abide within its own substance (*svabhāva*), because that own substance is definitively devoid of simultaneous arising and ceasing.
Therefore, it is unreasonable that visual consciousness should be perfumed by afflictions and secondary afflictions such as craving;
furthermore, this consciousness is not something that can be perfumed by consciousness.
As it has been said regarding visual consciousness, so it should be understood that the remaining evolving consciousnesses are likewise.

Furthermore, when one passes away from the higher stages such as the Realm of Non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) and is reborn in this world, the initial consciousness at that time—which is defiled by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—would have no seed. This is because both its support (*āśraya*) and its perfuming (*vāsanā*) have already passed away and lack any present existence.

Furthermore, when the consciousness that serves as the antidote to the afflictions has arisen and all other worldly consciousnesses have ceased, it would be illogical for the seeds of the remaining afflictions and secondary afflictions to reside within this antidotal consciousness if the ālayavijñāna were absent.

Because this counteractive consciousness is liberated by its very nature and does not arise or cease simultaneously with other afflictions or secondary afflictions, when a subsequent worldly consciousness arises later on, if the ālayavijñāna were absent, those various latencies (*vāsanā*) and their basis would have long since passed away and would no longer exist in the present; thus, there would be no seeds for it to arise again.
Therefore, if one were separated from the ālayavijñāna, the defilement of afflictions (kleśa-saṃkleśa) could not be established at all.
How is it that the defilement of karma (karma-saṃkleśa) cannot be established?
Because it would be inconsistent for volitional formations (saṃskāra) to serve as the condition for consciousness (vijñāna).
If this [appropriation] were non-existent, then existence conditioned by appropriation would also be inconsistent.
How, then, would the defilement of birth fail to be established?
Because it would be inconsistent with the moment of linking the continuity of rebirth.

If one dies from a state that is not in meditative equipoise and is reborn, the defiled mental consciousness arises based on the mind of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to effect the continuity of rebirth. This defiled mental consciousness ceases within the intermediate state, and the consciousness and the *kalala* (embryonic mass) coalesce within the mother’s womb.

If the mental consciousness itself were to conjoin with that [intermediate state], then once conjoined, this consciousness would serve as the basis for the arising of mental consciousness within the mother’s womb.
If that were so, there would necessarily be two mental consciousnesses arising simultaneously within the mother’s womb.

Furthermore, it is illogical for the consciousness that is conjoined with those [afflictions] to be of the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it would depend on defilement, because its occurrence would be uninterrupted, and because the objects of mental consciousness could not be apprehended.

If the consciousness that arises through conjunction is indeed the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), does this mental consciousness of conjunction itself constitute the storehouse consciousness (sarvabījaka-vijñāna),
or is it the other mental consciousnesses produced based upon this [storehouse] consciousness that constitute the storehouse consciousness?

If this combined consciousness (*saṃhatavijñāna*) is the all-seed consciousness, it is precisely the ālayavijñāna, which you have established as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) under a different name.

If the dependent consciousness (*āśrayavijñāna*) is the all-seed consciousness, then the supporting causal consciousness would not be the all-seed consciousness, while the supported resultant consciousness would be the all-seed consciousness; this is illogical.

Therefore, this consciousness that accomplishes this synthesis is not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), but is rather the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which is the consciousness of all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, once the connection to a new birth has been established, if one were apart from the maturation-consciousness, the appropriation of the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) would also be impossible.
Because the other various consciousnesses each have their own distinct bases and are not stable, these material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) should not be separated from consciousness.

If they were separated from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the mutual dependence of consciousness and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—which proceeds like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another—would also be untenable.
If one were apart from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) would not be established for sentient beings already born. Why is this?
Because it is impossible for any one of the six consciousnesses, taken individually, to perform the function of nutriment for sentient beings already born within the three realms.

If, upon passing away from this state and being reborn in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*), one undergoes the continuity of rebirth through a non-equipoised, defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then apart from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), no other entity consisting of seeds for that non-equipoised, defiled mind—which is subsumed within that [equipoised] stage—can possibly be found.

Furthermore, for those born in the formless realm, if the maturation consciousness containing all seeds were absent, then defiled and wholesome minds would lack their seeds, and defiled and wholesome minds would lack their support.

Furthermore, when supramundane consciousness is actually present within that very state, because all other mundane minds have been extinguished, one should at that time be extinguished from and depart from those realms of existence.

If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, when a supramundane mind of the sphere of nothingness manifests before one, then both destinies should be entirely extinguished and abandoned.

This supramundane consciousness does not take the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its basis, nor should it take the sphere of nothingness as its basis, nor does it take nirvana as its basis.

Furthermore, at the time of death, whether one has performed virtuous or non-virtuous deeds, and whether the physical basis (the body) cools from the bottom up or from the top down, none of these would be possible if the ālayavijñāna did not exist.
Therefore, if one were separated from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which contains all seeds, the defilement (*saṃkleśa*) of this birth would also be impossible to establish.
How, then, would the mundane purification (*viśuddhi*) not be established?

This refers to one who has not yet abandoned the greed associated with the desire realm and has not yet attained a mind associated with the form realm; such a person, for the sake of abandoning the greed associated with the desire realm, diligently cultivates preparatory application by means of a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm.

Since this preparatory mind bound to the desire realm does not arise and cease simultaneously with a mind bound to the form realm, it is not perfumed by the latter; therefore, it is unreasonable for it to serve as the seed for that [form-realm mind].

Furthermore, since the mind bound by the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) of past lives has been separated from the present concentrated mind by many intervening moments of other minds, it cannot serve as the seed for this present concentrated mind, simply because it no longer exists.

Therefore, it is established that the *vipākaphala-vijñāna* containing all seeds, which has been transmitted through successive stages, serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the present concentrated mind;
the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
In this manner, it should be understood that all stages of detachment from desire are likewise [impossible] without it.
Thus, such mundane purification cannot logically be established if the maturation consciousness containing all seeds is absent.
How is it that supramundane purity is not established?

It is because the Blessed One has taught that, based on the speech and sounds of others as well as one's own internal correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), right view arises with these as its causes.
Regarding these sounds of another's speech, when one attends to them appropriately (yoniśo-manasikāra), do they perfume the auditory consciousness (śrotra-vijñāna),
or do they perfume the mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna), or do they perfume both?
If one reflects upon those phenomena in accordance with reality, at that time auditory consciousness cannot arise;
furthermore, mental consciousness is interrupted by various other scattered and distracted cognitions.

If it arises in association with correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*), how can this consciousness—which is perfumed by hearing and whose perfuming has long since ceased and passed away, and which certainly lacks any substantial entity—again serve as the seed capable of producing a mind associated with correct mental attention at a later time?

Furthermore, this mind associated with correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*) is a worldly mind, whereas that [mind] associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is a supramundane mind; they have never arisen or ceased simultaneously. Therefore, this mind is not perfumed by that [supramundane mind].
Since it cannot be perfumed, it is illogical for it to serve as their seed.
Therefore, supramundane purity cannot be established if it is separated from the maturation-consciousness that contains all seeds.
In this context, it is because the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) is incompatible with the appropriation of those seeds.

Furthermore, how can the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which possesses all seeds and serves as the cause of defilement, also serve as the seed for the supramundane mind that acts as its antidote?
Furthermore, since supramundane mind has never been practiced in the past, its habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) must certainly be non-existent; if there is no perfuming, from what seed could it arise?
Therefore, one should answer:
it arises from seeds of the perfuming of correct hearing that flow forth from the most pure *dharmadhātu*.
Is this perfuming by hearing the intrinsic nature of the ālayavijñāna,
or is it not the intrinsic nature of the ālayavijñāna?
If it were the intrinsic nature of the ālayavijñāna, how could it be the seed for its own antidote?
If it were not of the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*, how could the basis for these seeds of the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) be perceived?

Up until the attainment of the bodhi of all Buddhas, these seeds of the perfuming of hearing abide in whichever of the various bases they may be active; they reside within the *vipākavijñāna*, evolving in conjunction with it and blending together like water and milk.
Nevertheless, they are not the *ālayavijñāna* itself, because they are of the nature of seeds that serve as its antidote.

In this context, based on inferior-grade perfuming, middle-grade perfuming is established; based on middle-grade perfuming, superior-grade perfuming is established; for by relying extensively upon hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one attains correspondence with the practice.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these seeds of the perfuming of correct hearing—in their inferior, middling, and superior grades—are also seeds of the Dharmakāya. They are contrary to the ālayavijñāna and are not subsumed within the ālayavijñāna; because they are of the nature of the outflow from the most pure supramundane dharmadhātu, although they are mundane, they possess the nature of seeds for the supramundane mind.

Furthermore, although the supramundane mind has not yet arisen, it is already able to counteract the entanglements of all afflictions, to counteract all perilous and evil destinies, and to act as the remedy that causes all existing evil karma to decay; moreover, it is able to accord with and serve all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Although these belong to the mundane world, it should be understood that what is attained by a bodhisattva who is newly engaged in practice is also subsumed within the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
That which is attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is subsumed solely within the liberation-body (*vimuktikāya*).
Furthermore, this perfuming is not the ālayavijñāna; it is subsumed within the dharmakāya and the vimuktikāya.

As the perfuming gradually increases through the stages of inferior, medium, and superior, so too does the resultant ripening consciousness (vipākaphala-vijñāna) gradually diminish, whereby the basis is transformed.
Once the basis has been transformed in every respect, the maturation-consciousness and all its seeds then proceed without seeds, and all seeds are forever severed.
Furthermore, how is it that they are like water and milk?
How is it that while the non-ālayavijñāna and the ālayavijñāna evolve together in the same location, all seeds of the ālayavijñāna are exhausted while all seeds of the non-ālayavijñāna increase?
It is like a swan drinking milk from water;

likewise, when one attains freedom from desire in the world, the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the non-meditative states gradually diminish, while the latencies of the meditative states gradually increase, whereby the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is attained.
Furthermore, it is taught by the Noble Ones that consciousness does not depart from the body when one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
In this context, the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) must be what does not depart from the body, for this attainment does not arise as an antidote to it.

Furthermore, this consciousness does not arise again upon emerging from meditative absorption, because once the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) has been interrupted, it cannot be regenerated without the reconnection of the stream of existence (*pratisaṃdhi*).

Moreover, the claim that the mind exists in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by virtue of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is untenable: for such an attainment would not be possible; its objects and modes of activity (*ālambana-ākāra*) could not be apprehended;

it would entail the fault of being associated with wholesome roots; it would be illogical for it to be unwholesome or neutral; it would entail the fault of the actual functioning (*samudācāra*) of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedanā*); contact (*sparśa*) would be perceivable; it would possess functional efficacy within the meditative concentration (*samādhi*); it would entail the fault of being merely the cessation of perception; it would entail the fault of the actual functioning of volition (*cetanā*), faith (*śraddhā*), and other wholesome roots; it would be illogical to extract the supported [consciousness] while leaving the support [the body] behind; there is a supporting analogy; and like those that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), it would not be present.

Furthermore, regarding those who maintain that there is a mind within this meditative absorption due to the presence of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), such a mind—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—cannot be established; therefore, their position is irrational.
Furthermore, if there is another who maintains that form and mind arise in immediate succession as the seeds of all phenomena, this cannot be established, as has already been explained previously.

Moreover, it would be illogical for this to be the case when one passes away from the formless realms or the heaven of non-perception, or upon emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the final mind of an Arhat cannot be established [as a cause for a subsequent state], as it can only admit of an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Thus, if one were to exclude the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which contains all seeds, neither defilement nor purification could be established. Therefore, the ālayavijñāna, possessing the characteristics previously described, is definitively proven to exist.
Regarding this, there are three verses:
"When a Bodhisattva, within the pure mind, Is far removed from the five consciousnesses without remainder,
And the mind undergoes transformation— how could you possibly do so?"
If the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) were merely the counteractive [path], it would not be established because it is not a cessation;
there would be no distinction between cause and fruit, and this would result in the fault that [the seeds] are never truly abandoned.
If one asserts that the transformation of the basis consists in the absence of seeds or the absence of an entity, [this is untenable].
"Because those two do not exist, the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) would be illogical.
Furthermore, what are the distinctions of this ālayavijñāna?
Briefly stated, it should be understood as being either threefold or fourfold.
Regarding these three types, they refer to the distinctions among the three kinds of habitual perfuming (vāsanā):

first, the distinction of the habitual perfuming of names and language; second, the distinction of the habitual perfuming of the view of self; and third, the distinction of the habitual perfuming of the links of existence (bhavāṅga).

The four kinds are: first, the differentiation of production; second, the differentiation of maturation; third, the differentiation of causal characteristics; and fourth, the differentiation of appearances.
Regarding the differentiation of production herein, it refers to the newly arising perfuming.
If this did not exist, then the condition of formative action for consciousness and the condition of grasping for existence would be unable to be established.

Regarding the differentiation of maturation (*vipāka*) therein: it refers to the differentiation of maturation within the various realms of existence (*gati*) conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*).
If this [storehouse consciousness] were non-existent, there would be no seed, and consequently, the arising of all phenomena in future existence (*punarbhava*) would be impossible.
Regarding the distinction of the objective aspect (*nimitta*) herein: it refers to the objective aspect of the grasping at a self within the manas.
If this were non-existent, the objective referent (*ālambana*) for the grasping at a self within the afflicted manas would be impossible to establish.
Regarding the distinctions among its characteristics herein:

it refers to the fact that this very consciousness possesses both common characteristics and non-common characteristics, as well as characteristics of seeds for the production of non-sentient experience and characteristics of seeds for the production of sentient experience, and so forth.
The common characteristic refers to the seeds of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The uncommon characteristic refers to the seeds of the individual internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
The common characteristic is the seed for birth without sensation (*anupabhoga*), while the uncommon characteristic is the seed for birth with sensation (*sopabhoga*).
When the antidote arises, only that which is to be countered by its unique characteristic (asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa) is extinguished.

As for common characteristics (sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa), they are maintained by the conceptual constructions of others; thus, one perceives only purity, just as yogins, through various degrees of resolve (adhimukti) regarding a single object, each establish their own various perceptions.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"Difficult to sever and difficult to fully know, They should be known as common fetters;
The minds of practitioners differ Because external signs are so vast."
"Although purity does not cease, one perceives purity therein;
likewise, the pure Buddha-fields appear pure because the Buddha perceives them as such.
Furthermore, there is another verse:
The various types of resolute conviction and the various types of perception cited above are all established.
"Yogins, with respect to a single object, Have diverse resolute convictions, each different;
Their various perceptions are all established; Therefore, one knows that what is apprehended exists only as consciousness."
If this did not exist, the various distinctions in the arising of the receptacle world and the sentient world would be impossible to establish.
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness/heaviness) and *praśrabdhi* (pliancy/lightness):
the characteristic of *dauṣṭhulya* refers to the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The characteristic of pliancy refers to the seeds of contaminated wholesome phenomena.
If these were absent, the resultant maturation would lack functional capacity; thus, the differentiation of the basis that possesses such functional capacity could not be established.
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of the exhaustion of feeling and the characteristics of the non-exhaustion of feeling:
that which has the characteristic of the exhaustion of feeling refers to the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma whose ripened fruits have already matured.

The characteristic of the exhaustion of experience refers to the seeds of the perfuming of names and words, for they are the seeds of the various conceptual proliferations that have circulated since beginningless time.
If these were non-existent, then the exhaustion of the results of the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—already performed would be impossible to establish.
Furthermore, the arising of newly acquired linguistic designations (*nāma-vyavahāra*) through perfuming (*vāsanā*) would be impossible.
Moreover, there is the characteristic of being illustrated by analogies:
namely, that this ālayavijñāna is illustrated by the analogies of a magical illusion, a mirage, a dream, and a visual impairment.
If this were non-existent, then because it would lack the seeds of unreal universal imagination (*parikalpita*), the correspondence with inverted conditions could not be established.
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of being complete and the characteristics of being incomplete:
those who are bound by all fetters are said to possess the characteristics of completeness.
Those in the world who have abandoned desire are said to possess the characteristic of diminished [defilements].
Śrāvakas in training and all Bodhisattvas are said to possess the characteristic of having permanently uprooted a portion [of defilements].

Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Tathāgatas are said to possess the characteristic of having completely and permanently uprooted the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the characteristic of having completely and permanently uprooted both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as appropriate to each case. If these did not exist, the successive cessation of the various forms of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) would be impossible to accomplish.
For what reason do wholesome and unwholesome dharmas produce maturation, yet their maturation fruit is non-obscured and neutral?

It is because the non-obscured, neutral maturation fruit is not mutually contradictory with the wholesome and unwholesome, whereas the wholesome and unwholesome are mutually contradictory with one another.
If the ripening fruit were of a wholesome or unwholesome nature, the cessation of affliction would be impossible; therefore, the ripening consciousness is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate.

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Three:
The Characteristics of the Knowable. The basis of the knowable has already been explained. How, then, should the characteristics of the knowable be contemplated?
Briefly, there are three kinds:
first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*); second, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Among these, what is the dependent nature?
This refers to the various consciousnesses comprised within false discrimination, which have the ālayavijñāna as their seed.
Furthermore, what are these? They are:

the body, the possessor of the body, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of that which is experienced, the consciousness of the experiencer thereof, the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, the consciousness of verbal expression, the consciousness of the distinction between self and other, and the consciousness of death and birth in good and evil destinies.

In this context, the body, the experiencer of the body, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of that which is experienced, the consciousness of the experiencer [of that], the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, and the consciousness of verbal expression—these arise from the seeds of the perfuming of names and expressions.
If it is the consciousness of the distinction between self and others, this arises from the seeds perfumed by the view of self.
If it is the consciousness of death and birth in the happy or miserable realms, this arises from the seeds perfumed by the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

By means of these various consciousnesses, all that is comprised within the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*)—the false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) subsumed under the defilements of all realms and destinies—is made manifest.

These various consciousnesses are all comprised within false discrimination; they have the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), and they are the basis for the manifestation of non-existent and unreal objects.
This is called the dependent nature.
In this context, what is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?
It is the appearance of objects within that which is merely consciousness and devoid of external objects.
In this context, what is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?
This refers to the fact that within that very other-dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), the appearance of objects is eternally devoid of intrinsic existence.
Herein, "body," "possessor of the body," and "experiencer-consciousness" should be understood as the six internal bases (*āyatana*), such as the eye and so forth.
That consciousness which is the object of experience should be understood as the six external spheres, such as form and so forth.
That consciousness which is the subject of experience should be understood as the six consciousness spheres, such as eye-consciousness and so forth.
It should be understood that the remaining consciousnesses are merely specific variations of these [eight] consciousnesses.
Furthermore, all these consciousnesses consist of nothing but consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), because they are entirely devoid of external objects.
By what analogy is this demonstrated?
It should be understood that dreams and the like are presented as metaphors to demonstrate this.

That is to say, just as in a dream there is no external object whatsoever, but only consciousness alone; although various forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, as well as houses, forests, lands, and mountains, appear as reflections of objects, yet within these there is no object at all.
By means of this analogy, one should understand accordingly that at all times and in all places there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), it should be understood that there are further analogies such as illusions, mirages, and visual distortions.

If, during the waking state, at all times and in all places, everything is like a dream and consists of nothing but consciousness, then just as one realizes upon waking from a dream that everything within the dream consisted of nothing but consciousness, why does such a realization not occur during the waking state?
The transformation of true wisdom upon awakening is likewise:

just as this awakening does not occur while one is dreaming, but only occurs upon waking from the dream, so too, this awakening does not occur before one has attained the awakening of true wisdom, but only occurs once true wisdom is attained.
For those who have not yet attained the awakening of true wisdom, how can they infer [the nature of] representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*)?
It should be inferred through both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
Regarding scripture here, as the Blessed One said in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
"Thus, these three realms are all merely mind.
Furthermore, the Blessed One speaks likewise in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. In that sūtra, the Bodhisattva Maitreya asks the Bhagavān:
"Regarding the images that are the objects of various samādhis, should it be said that they are different from this mind?"
"Should it be said that they are not different?
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"It should be said that they are not different. Why is this so?"
"Because those images are nothing but consciousness;
therefore, I say that the object of consciousness is manifested solely by consciousness.
"World-Honored One!"
"If the image traversed in samādhi is not different from this mind itself, how can this mind take this very mind as its object?
"Maitreya! [The Blessed One replied:]
There is not even the slightest dharma that can grasp another dharma; nevertheless, when this very mind arises in such a way, an image corresponding to it appears.

It is like seeing a physical object as the condition for perceiving that very object, yet thinking, "I am now seeing an image," and thinking that an image appears as something seen apart from the object itself.
This mind is likewise; when it arises in such a manner, there appears a reflection that seems similar yet different.
This is also manifested by this very teaching and reasoning. Why is this so?

Within the state of meditative concentration, whatever known images one perceives—such as the various forms of bluish discoloration and so forth—are entirely nothing other than the bluish discolorations themselves; they are merely the seeing of one's own mind.
By this reasoning, a bodhisattva should infer through analogy that within all consciousness there is only consciousness and no external objects.

Furthermore, in the case of such things as the livid corpse and so forth, it is not a memory-consciousness (*smṛti-vijñāna*) that perceives the perceived object, because [the object] is present before one.

The two types of recollective consciousnesses produced through hearing and reflection also take the past as their object; therefore, the images that appear are established as being representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
By means of this inference, although a bodhisattva has not yet attained the awakening of true wisdom, they should be able to infer [the nature of reality] within the context of representation-only.

Thus, having already explained the various consciousnesses through analogies such as dreams and the like, it is established that within this context, the eye-consciousness and other such cognitions are mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). However, since the eyes and other sense organs are material in nature, how can it be seen that they too are nothing but consciousness?
This is also as previously explained through scripture and reasoning.
If these various consciousnesses are also in essence consciousness, why do they manifest as having the nature of form (*rūpa*), appearing as a uniform, stable, and continuous stream?
Because it serves as the basis for various defiled phenomena such as the perversions;
otherwise, the perversion that conceives of non-objects as objects would not be possible.
If this did not exist, the defilements of the two obstacles—those of afflictions and those of the cognizable—would be impossible.
If this did not exist, all pure phenomena would likewise be non-existent.
Therefore, the various consciousnesses should transform in this manner.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"The disordered appearance and the disordered essence Should be admitted as the consciousness of form."
"And as for non-material consciousness, if one is absent, the other is also absent. Why is this?

Because the body-consciousness (*deha-vijñāna*), the owner-of-the-body-consciousness (*dehin-vijñāna*), the experiencer-consciousness (*upabhoktṛ-vijñāna*), the consciousness of what is experienced (*upabhogyavijñāna*), and the consciousness that experiences (*upabhogavijñāna*) all function in conjunction and in harmony within every body, being able to fully manifest the arising of experience and enjoyment.
For what reason do the various consciousnesses, such as those of the world and so forth, evolve with their respective distinctions?
Because the cycle of birth and death has been in continuous flux since beginningless time;
and because the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable and infinite.
Because the various receptacle worlds are immeasurable;
because the successive verbal explanations of all activities performed therein are immeasurable;
and because the distinct apprehensions and enjoyments of their differences are immeasurable.

Because there are immeasurable distinctions in the enjoyment of the maturation of the fruits of various pleasant and unpleasant karmas, and because there are immeasurable distinctions in the various births and deaths one undergoes.
Furthermore, how are these various consciousnesses established as being the nature of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā)?
Briefly, it is by way of three characteristics:
first, by way of representation-only, because there are no external objects.
2. By way of duality, because there is the distinction between the two consciousnesses of the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*);
3. By way of variety, because it arises with various modes of activity (*ākāra*).
Why is this so? Because all these consciousnesses lack external objects, they are established as "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
Because they possess the aspects (nimitta) and the seeing (darśana), they are established as being twofold.

If the visual consciousness and the others take the consciousnesses of form and so forth as their objective aspect (*nimitta*) and the cognition of the visual consciousness as their seeing (*darśana*),
up to the cognition of the tactile consciousness as their seeing;

and if the mental consciousness takes all consciousnesses— from the visual consciousness as the first to the consciousness of phenomena (*dharma*) as the last— as their objective aspect and the cognition of the mental consciousness as its seeing.
Because this mental consciousness possesses discrimination and arises as if it were all other forms of cognition,
there is a verse on this point:
"The two kinds of representation-only, The contemplator’s mind can enter."
"By realizing that there is only mind, one is likewise able to subdue and depart from them.

Furthermore, within this context, there is a class of masters who assert a single consciousness which, as it evolves in dependence upon various bases, receives various names—just as mental karma is designated by the names "bodily karma" and "vocal karma."
Furthermore, when all bases (āśraya) function, two kinds of images appear as various characteristics:
namely, the image of the object alone and the image of conceptualization.

Furthermore, in all places, it also manifests as an image resembling the tangible; within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this very mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) relies upon the body, just as the other material sense-faculties rely upon the body.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"If one travels far, wanders alone, Sleeps in the cave without a body,
And tames this mind so difficult to tame— I call him a true brahmin."
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"The objects traversed by these five faculties are each received by the mind; the mind is their support.
Also, as stated among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the six groups of consciousness are all called the mind base (*manāyatana*).

If, in a certain context, the *ālaya-vijñāna* is established as the "object-consciousness" (*artha-vijñapti*), it should be understood that all other consciousnesses therein are its "image-consciousness" (*nimitta-vijñapti*), while the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) and its support are its "perceiving-consciousness" (*darśana-vijñapti*). This is because that image-consciousness serves as the causal condition for the arising of this perceiving-consciousness; thus, when appearing as an object, it performs the function of providing a basis for the arising of the perceiving-consciousness.
This is what is called establishing the various consciousnesses as the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
How can it be known that although all objects appear before one and manifest with great clarity, they do not exist?
As the Blessed One said:
"If bodhisattvas accomplish four dharmas, they are able to realize accordingly that all is representation-only and that external objects do not exist at all.

First, they accomplish the wisdom of the characteristics of contradictory cognitions; for example, hungry ghosts, animals, and gods and humans alike perceive the same object, yet there are differences in what each cognizes."

Second, one achieves the wisdom that cognitions can be perceived even when they lack an objective referent (*anālambana*), because objects are apprehended within conditions such as the past, the future, dreams, and reflections.

Third, one achieves the wisdom that is free from error without relying on effortful application; for if there were truly external objects, the cognitions perceiving those objects would have to be non-erroneous by nature, rather than being true only through the application of wisdom.
Fourth, they achieve the sublime wisdom that functions in accordance with the three kinds of supreme wisdom.
What are these three?

First, for all bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over the mind and have attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), objects appear in accordance with the power of their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
2. For one who has attained śamatha and practices the cultivation of insight (vipaśyanā), all objects appear as soon as they bring them to mind.
3. For one who has already attained non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna), when non-conceptual wisdom is present before them, no objects at all appear.

By means of these three types of superior wisdom that function in accordance with reality, as well as the three types of causes and conditions previously explained, the principles regarding what is meaningful and what is meaningless are established.

If the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is in reality nothing but consciousness, which serves as the basis for the manifestation of objects as if they were external, how does it become "dependent"?
For what reason and by what conditions is it called "dependent"?
It is called "other-dependent" (*paratantra*) because it arises from seeds produced by its own habitual perfuming and depends upon other conditions for its origination;
it is called "other-dependent" because, after the moment of its arising, it lacks the capacity to abide spontaneously.

If the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is that which appears as an object while being entirely non-existent based upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), how does it become the "thoroughly imagined"?
For what reason and by what conditions is it called the "thoroughly imagined"?
The consciousness that conceptualizes through infinite modes of activity arises as a state of perversion; therefore, it is called "the thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*).
Its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not exist in reality, and only that which is thoroughly imagined can be apprehended; for this reason, it is termed "the thoroughly imagined."

If the thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the permanent non-existence of the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), how does it become the thoroughly established nature?
By what causes and conditions is it called the "thoroughly established"?
It is called "thoroughly established" (pariniṣpanna) because it is unchanging;

furthermore, it is called "thoroughly established" in the sense of being the supreme object of purification and the most excellent nature among all wholesome dharmas. Thus, it is termed "thoroughly established" by virtue of its supreme meaning.

Furthermore, there is that which performs the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) and that which is the object of pervasive conceptualization; it is through these that the nature of what is grasped by pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is established.
In this context, what is that which performs the pervasive conceptualization?
What is that which is the object of pervasive conceptualization?
What is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva)?
One should know that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is that which performs pervasive conceptualization, because it possesses discrimination.

Why is this so? Because this mental consciousness takes as its seeds the habitual perfuming of its own names and phrases, as well as the habitual perfuming of the names and phrases of all [other] consciousnesses; therefore, mental consciousness evolves through infinite modes of conceptualization and operates universally across all forms of discursive construction and deliberation. For this reason, it is called "universal imagination" (*parikalpa*).
Furthermore, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is called the "object of universal conceptualization" (*parikalpya*).
Moreover, that characteristic by which the dependent nature is made into an object of universal conceptualization is here termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
"By these characteristics" means "in this manner.
Furthermore, how does the pervasive imagination (parikalpa) perform its pervasive conceptualization?
What is its objective sphere (ālambana)?
What characteristics are grasped?
By what is there attachment?
By what is speech produced?
By what means is verbal expression produced? What is it that is superimposed? It is as follows:

taking "name" as its object, one grasps its characteristics within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); through the adherence of views, through discursive thought (*vitarka*), and through the four kinds of verbal expression such as seeing and hearing, one produces speech. Within that which lacks objective reality, one superimposes existence; by means of this, the pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*) is able to perform universal conceptualization (*parikalpayati*).
