This very nature becomes the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) through a certain perspective; this very same nature becomes the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) through another perspective.
By what perspective does this *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) become the *paratantra-svabhāva*?
Because it arises from seeds perfumed by others,
by what distinct aspect does this very self-nature become the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature)?
It is because it is the characteristic (*nimitta*) that serves as the object of imagination, and because it is that which is imagined by the imagination.
By what alternative formulation does this very same intrinsic nature become the thoroughly established nature?
It is because that which is universally conceptualized is ultimately not existent in that way.
How many types are there for each of these three natures?
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is briefly of two kinds:

first, because it arises based on seeds of habitual perfuming; second, because its nature as either afflicted (*saṃkleśa*) or purified (*vyavadāna*) is not established independently. It is called "dependent" due to these two distinct types of dependence.
The thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is also of two kinds:
first, because of the thorough imagination of intrinsic nature; second, because of the thorough imagination of specific distinctions. For this reason, it is called the "thoroughly imagined nature."
The thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) also has two aspects:

first, because it is the thoroughly established nature by its very essence; second, because it is the thoroughly established nature through purification. It is by virtue of these that it constitutes the thoroughly established nature.
Furthermore, there are four types of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*):

first, pervasive conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, pervasive conceptualization of specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*); third, pervasive conceptualization with awareness (*sa-vitarka*); and fourth, pervasive conceptualization without awareness (*a-vitarka*).
Those with discernment refer to those skilled in linguistic expression;
those without discernment refer to those unskilled in linguistic expression.
Thus, there are five further types of pervasive conceptualization:
1. Universal conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of objects based on names, meaning that such-and-such an object exists for such-and-such a name;
2. Universal conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of names based on objects, meaning that such-and-such a name exists for such-and-such an object;
3. Universal conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of names based on names, meaning the conceptualization of names whose referents are not yet understood.
Fourth, the imagined nature of objects based on objects (*artha*), which refers to the conceptualization of objects whose names have not yet been understood;
fifth, the imagined nature of both based on both, which refers to the conceptualization that "this name has such-and-such an essence as its object."
Furthermore, there are briefly ten types that encompass all forms of conceptualization (*vikalpa*):
first, fundamental conceptualization, which refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna*;
second, conceptualization of objective signs, which refers to the consciousnesses of form and so forth.
Third, the discrimination of manifest characteristics, which refers to the eye-consciousness and so forth, together with their supporting consciousnesses.

Fourth, the discrimination of the transformation of objective conditions, which refers to transformations such as aging and so forth; transformations of pleasant feelings and so forth; transformations of greed and so forth; transformations due to affliction, seasonal changes, and the passage of time; transformations among the various destinies such as the hells (*nāraka*) and so forth; and transformations among the various realms such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.
Fifth, the discrimination of the variation of manifest characteristics, which refers to all variations of the aforementioned variations.
Sixth, the discrimination induced by others, which refers to the discrimination arising from hearing categories of non-orthodox teachings as well as hearing categories of orthodox teachings.
7. Irrational discrimination refers to the discrimination of those non-Buddhists who hear what is not the true Dharma.
8. Rational discrimination refers to the discrimination within the true Dharma of those who hear the true Dharma.

Ninth, clinging discrimination refers to the class of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), specifically the discrimination associated with the sixty-two views, which have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their basis.
10. Distraction and Discursive Differentiation (*vikṣepa-vikalpa*): This refers to the ten kinds of discursive differentiation of Bodhisattvas:

(1) distraction regarding the signless (*animitta*), (2) distraction regarding the signed (*sanimitta*), (3) distraction through superimposition (*samāropa*), (4) distraction through negation (*apavāda*), (5) distraction regarding identity (*ekatva*), (6) distraction regarding difference (*nānātva*), (7) distraction regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), (8) distraction regarding specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*), (9) distraction that grasps the object according to the name (*yathā-nāma-artha-udgraha*), and (10) distraction that grasps the name according to the object (*yathārtha-nāma-udgraha*).
To counteract these ten types of distraction, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is taught throughout all the *prajñāpāramitā* scriptures.
One should understand that this relationship between the objects to be countered and their remedies fully encompasses the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If, by way of different perspectives (*paryāya*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) possesses three natures, how is it that these three natures do not become indistinguishable?
If it is established as the dependent nature by one perspective, it is not thereby established as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) or the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
if it is established as the imagined nature by another perspective, it is not thereby established as the dependent nature or the perfected nature.
If something is established as the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* from one perspective, it is not thereby established as the *paratantra-svabhāva* or the *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
Furthermore, how is it known that the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, while appearing like the *paratantra-svabhāva*, does not correspond to its actual essence?
Because there is no cognition [of an object] prior to its name, it contradicts the claim that the name conforms to the essence;
because names are manifold, it contradicts the claim that there is a multiplicity of essences;
and because names are not fixed, it contradicts the claim that there is a mixture of essences.
In this regard, there are two verses:
"Because prior to a name, cognition does not exist; because of multiple names and lack of determination;
because it would entail identity with the name, multiplicity of entities, and confusion of characteristics—these contradictions [prove that things do not exist as they appear]."
"The dharmas are non-existent yet can be apprehended; they are without defilement yet possess purity.
One should know them to be like illusions and the like, and also resembling empty space.

Furthermore, for what reason is it that while that which is manifested as appearing is entirely non-existent, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is not entirely and in every respect non-existent?
If this [the dependent nature] did not exist, the perfected nature would also be non-existent;
if this were non-existent, then everything would be non-existent.
If the dependent nature and the perfected nature were non-existent, it would entail the fault that there is neither affliction nor purification.
Since both affliction and purification are actually observed to exist, it is not the case that everything is non-existent.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"If the dependent nature does not exist, The perfected nature also does not exist."
"If all aspects did not exist, there would never be defilement or purification.
In the Mahāyāna, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught the Vaipulya scriptures; therein it is said:
"How should one understand the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?"
One should understand that "non-existence" is taught through various alternative formulations (*paryāya*).
How should one understand the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
One should understand it to be like a magical illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an optical aberration, a shadow, an echo, the moon in water, and a transformation.
How should the thoroughly established nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) be understood?
It should be understood through the teaching of the four dharmas of purification.
What are these four dharmas of purification?

First is natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the signless (*animitta*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Second is purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*), which refers to this very same [nature] when it is free from all obstructive defilements.
Third is the purity of attaining this path, which refers to all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), and so forth.
Fourth is the purity of producing this object, which refers to the sublime and correct teachings of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Because this teaching of the Dharma serves as the cause for purification, it is not the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva);
because it is of the nature of the outflow from the most pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), it is not the nature of the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva).
"These four dharmas encompass all pure phenomena without exception.
Within this, there are two verses:
"The production [of things] is said to be like an illusion..."
The teaching that there is no grasping at what is imagined, and the teaching of the four purities, is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The intrinsic nature and the purity through removal of stains, as well as the objects of the path of purification—
all purified phenomena— are subsumed within these four characteristics.
Furthermore, for what reason are metaphors such as illusions taught regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as stated in the sūtras?
It is in order to eliminate the false doubts of others concerning the dependent nature.
Furthermore, how can there be false doubt regarding the dependent nature?
It is because others have such a doubt as this:
"How is it that although objects do not truly exist, they nevertheless become the objective spheres of experience?"
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of a magical illusion (*māyā*) is taught:
how can mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise in the absence of an external object?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of a mirage (*marīci*) is taught.
How can there be the distinction between the experience of the desirable and the undesirable when there is no external object?
To remove this doubt, the analogy of a dream is taught.
How can the distinction between the results of pure and impure karma—the desirable and the undesirable—arise if there is no external object?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of a reflection is taught.
To address the doubt as to how various cognitions can arise in the absence of external objects,
the analogy of light and shadow is taught.
How is it that various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and verbal expressions proceed despite being devoid of objective referents?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of an echo is taught.
How is it that there is a real apprehension of the objects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) proceeding despite their being devoid of objective referents?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of the moon in water is taught.

How can it be that there are bodhisattvas who, despite the absence of an objective referent, give rise to non-erroneous minds and intentionally undergo rebirth for the sake of accomplishing the various benefits and happiness of sentient beings?
To eliminate this doubt, the parable of the transformation is taught.
Based on what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) did the Blessed One state in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"The Tathāgata does not attain saṃsāra, nor does he attain nirvāṇa"?

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is the intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*) that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are without distinction, based upon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Why is this? It is because this very other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) constitutes saṃsāra through its aspect of the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), and constitutes nirvāṇa through its aspect of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
In the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra*, the Bhagavān says:
“There are three kinds of phenomena:
first, the defiled portion; second, the purified portion; and third, that which belongs to both portions.”
With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) was this said?

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) constitutes the defiled portion, while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) constitutes the purified portion; thus, the dependent nature itself consists of these two portions.
It is with this underlying intention that it was so stated.
By what analogy is this meaning illustrated?
It is illustrated by the analogy of a gold-bearing earth deposit.
For example, three things can be found within a worldly gold-bearing earth deposit:
There are three: first, the earth element; second, soil; and third, gold.
Within the earth element, soil is not substantially existent yet appears to be obtainable, whereas gold is substantially existent yet is not obtainable.
When subjected to the refining process of fire, the appearance of soil does not manifest, and the appearance of gold becomes manifest.

Furthermore, regarding this earth element, when it appears as soil, it is a false appearance; when it appears as gold, it is a true appearance. Therefore, the earth element consists of these two parts.

Consciousness is also like this: when the fire of non-conceptual wisdom has not yet burned it, all that appears within this consciousness is the false, imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while the true, perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) does not appear.

When this consciousness is incinerated by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), the true perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) within this consciousness manifests, while the false imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not manifest;
therefore, this consciousness of false discrimination, as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), possesses these two portions, just like the earth element within a deposit of gold and soil.

The Bhagavān has in some places taught that all phenomena are permanent, in some places taught that all phenomena are impermanent, and in some places taught that all phenomena are neither permanent nor impermanent. With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) did he speak thus?

This refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*): it is permanent in its aspect as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), impermanent in its aspect as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and neither permanent nor impermanent by virtue of those two aspects.
It is with this underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) that such a statement was made.
Just as permanence and impermanence are non-dual, so too are suffering and pleasure non-dual;
purity and impurity are non-dual;
emptiness and non-emptiness are non-dual.
Self and non-self are non-dual;
tranquility and non-tranquility are non-dual;
having intrinsic nature and lacking intrinsic nature are non-dual.
Arising and non-arising are non-dual;
cessation and non-cessation are non-dual;
primordial quiescence and the absence of primordial quiescence are non-dual.
Nirvana by nature and non-nirvana by nature are non-dual; likewise, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-dual.
Such distinctions—the intentional terminology of all Buddhas—should be understood according to the three natures, as previously explained through the categories of permanence and impermanence.
Regarding this, there are many verses:
"Just as phenomena do not exist in reality, yet appear in manifold ways;
they are neither phenomena nor non-phenomena—therefore, they are said to have the meaning of non-duality."
Based on one aspect, it is revealed as either existent or non-existent;
based on two aspects, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
Since it does not exist in the manner that it appears, it is therefore called "non-existent."
Because they appear in such a manner, they are said to exist.

Yet, being spontaneous, they lack an intrinsic essence; their self-nature does not endure, and since they do not exist in the way they are grasped, they are held to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
"Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, it is established as the support for each subsequent stage;
it is without arising or ceasing, primordially quiescent, and by its very nature in parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are four intentions and four secrets, through which all the Buddha’s words should be understood and resolved.
The four intentions (*abhiprāya*) are:
first, the intention of equality (*samatābhiprāya*), as when it is said:
"In that time and at that juncture, I was the perfectly awakened one named Vipaśyin."
2. The intention regarding another time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*) refers, for example, to the statement:
"If one recites the name of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, one has already attained certainty regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, as it is said:
"By merely making a vow, one attains rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
Third, the intentional meaning regarding a specific sense (*paryāyābhiprāya*), which refers, for example, to what is said:
"If one has already served as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, only then can one understand the meaning of the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Fourth is the *pudgalāśayābhiprāya* (the intention regarding the inclinations of individuals), which refers, for example, to first praising generosity for a certain individual and later disparaging it;
as it is with generosity, so it should be understood for ethical discipline (*śīla*) and a portion of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
These are called the four intentions (*abhiprāya*).
As for the four secrets (*saṃdhi*):

first, the secret of leading [others] into [the teaching], which refers to the teaching that, within either the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Mahāyāna, there exist persons (*pudgala*) and the distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of phenomena (*dharma*) based on the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
2. The secret of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-guhyaka*) refers to those instances where the characteristics of all phenomena are taught to reveal the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
3. The secret of antidotes (*pratipakṣa-guhyaka*) refers to those instances where the eighty-four thousand practices that serve as antidotes are taught.
Fourth is the secret of transformation (*pariṇāma-guhya*). This refers to instances where, through a specific intended meaning, various words and syllables manifest a distinct significance.
As a verse says:
"Perceiving the non-solid as solid, Abiding well within inversion..."
"Though afflicted by the most extreme afflictions, one attains supreme enlightenment.
If one wishes to compose an exposition on the Mahāyāna Dharma, that exposition should briefly be composed by means of three aspects:
first, by explaining dependent origination; second, by explaining the characteristics of phenomena produced from conditions; and third, by explaining the meaning of the words.
Regarding the explanation of dependent origination herein, it is said:
"Phenomena produced by the perfuming of speech arise from that;
The ripening consciousness and the evolving consciousnesses Arise as mutual conditions for one another."

Furthermore, those phenomena characterized by the evolving consciousnesses possess the image-aspect (*nimitta*), the seeing-aspect (*darśana*), and have consciousness as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Moreover, they take the locus of support as their characteristic, the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*) as their characteristic, and the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as their characteristic; by this, the characteristics of the three natures are revealed.
As it is said:
"From the characteristic of existence, there is seeing; one should know those three characteristics.
Furthermore, how should those characteristics be explained?
This means that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) is utterly non-existent within the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*),
whereas the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) truly exists therein.
Due to these two aspects— non-existence and existence, or non-attainment and attainment— the one who has not yet seen and the one who has already seen the truth act simultaneously.
This means that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is absent and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is present,
when one realizes the former, one does not realize the latter, and when one realizes the latter, one does not realize the former.
As it is said:
"The dependent nature lacks the imagined; within it, the perfected nature exists.
Therefore, attainment and non-attainment are both equal therein."

Regarding the explanation of the meaning of the words: this refers to first stating the initial phrase and subsequently analyzing and clarifying it through subsequent phrases, either by way of its qualities (*guṇa*) or by way of its meaning (*artha*).
Regarding the basis of qualities, it refers to the explanation of the Buddha’s qualities:
his most pure awakening; the non-dual manifestation; his progression toward the signless dharma; his abiding in the Buddha-abode;
his attainment of the equality of all Buddhas; his arrival at the state of non-obstruction; and his unshakeable dharma.
Their conduct is unimpeded, and their established state is inconceivable; they traverse the equal dharma-nature of the three periods of time, and their bodies are distributed throughout all worlds.
Regarding all dharmas, their wisdom is free from doubt or obstruction;
regarding all practices, they have achieved great awakening; regarding the wisdom of all dharmas, they possess no uncertainty. Whatever...
His manifested body is beyond conceptual differentiation; he has attained the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas alike, reaching the supreme further shore of the Buddha’s non-dual dwelling.
His wondrous wisdom of Tathāgata-liberation is ultimate and unmixed;
he realizes the equality of the Buddha-ground, which is without center or periphery, extending to the limit of the dharma-realm, exhausting the nature of space, and reaching the end of the future.

Regarding the phrase "the most pure awakening," it should be understood that this phrase is analytically revealed by the remaining phrases; in this way, the nature of the well-expounded Dharma is established.
"Most pure awakening" refers to the most pure awakening of the Buddha, the World-Honored One; it should be understood as being comprised of twenty-one qualities of a Buddha.
These are: the quality of proceeding toward the objects of knowledge with absolute absence of obstruction;

the quality of being able to enter the most supreme purity of suchness, which is free from the two characteristics of existence and non-existence; and the quality of abiding without cessation in effortless buddha-activities.
The merit of the non-differentiation of the basis, intention, and activity within the dharmakāya; the merit of cultivating remedies for all obstacles;
the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists; the merit of being born in the world without being hindered by worldly phenomena;
the merit of establishing the true Dharma; and the merit of bestowing predictions of enlightenment.
The merit of manifesting the enjoyment and transformation bodies in all worlds;
the merit of severing doubt; the merit of causing entry into various practices; the merit of generating sublime wisdom regarding future phenomena;
the merit of manifesting according to [beings'] inclinations; the merit of the application for taming sentient beings through immeasurable bases; and the merit of impartiality.
The merit of fulfilling the perfections of the *dharmakāya*; the merit of manifesting diverse buddha-fields according to the inclinations of beings;
the merit of the three bodies of the Buddha being without spatial limitation;
the merit of constantly appearing to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings until the end of cyclic existence; and the merit of inexhaustibility, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the basis of meaning, it is as stated:
"If bodhisattvas accomplish thirty-two qualities, they are then called 'bodhisattvas.
That is to say, because they give rise to the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings."
In order to cause [beings] to enter the knowledge of all-knowledge; because they know for themselves what provisional wisdom they currently possess;

because they have subdued pride; because their superior intention is firm and steadfast; because their compassion is not merely provisional; because they maintain a mind of equanimity toward both friends and enemies;
because they act as true spiritual friends until the very end of *nirvāṇa*; and because they act with appropriate measure—
Because he speaks with a smile and initiates conversation; because he possesses boundless great compassion;
because he never falters or weakens in the tasks he has undertaken; because he is free from weariness; because he never tires of hearing the Dharma;
because he perceives his own transgressions as deep faults; because he instructs others for their transgressions without anger; and regarding all modes of conduct...
Because they constantly cultivate and purify the bodhicitta; because they practice generosity without desiring karmic maturation;

because they uphold the precepts without depending on any state of existence within the realms of rebirth; because they practice patience without harboring anger or obstruction toward sentient beings;
because they exert diligence in order to embrace all wholesome dharmas; and because they abandon the formless realm while practicing meditation.
Because of meditative concentration; because of cultivating wisdom in conjunction with skillful means; because of gathering [beings] through the four means of attraction as skillful means;
because of being without dualism toward virtuous friends who maintain the precepts or violate them; because of listening to the true Dharma with a sincere and earnest mind;
because of dwelling in forest hermitages with a sincere and earnest mind; and because of having no fondness for worldly distractions.
Therefore, because they have never taken pleasure in the inferior vehicles, because they perceive the profound merits within the Mahāyāna,
because they distance themselves from evil friends and draw near to virtuous friends, because they constantly cultivate and purify the four Brahma-abodes,
because they perpetually sport in the five supernormal powers, and because they rely upon wisdom, they remain steadfast in right practice.
Because they do not abandon those sentient beings who abide in right practice, because their words are definitive, because they revere truth and reality,
and because the great bodhicitta is always held as foremost.
It should be understood that all these phrases are variations of the first phrase;
namely, the superior intention (adhyāśaya) to bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
It should be understood that these phrases concerning the superior intention for benefit and happiness consist of sixteen distinct types of activity.
Among them, the sixteen activities are:
first, the activity of successive application;
2. Unmistaken activity;
3. Spontaneous activity that does not depend on being requested by others;
4. Immovable and indestructible activity;

5. Action free from seeking defilement; this should be understood as having three distinct aspects: namely, because it is untainted by attachment; because it is free from love and hatred toward both benefactors and non-benefactors; and because it persists continuously throughout successive births.
6. Corresponding verbal and bodily action; this should be understood as having two distinct aspects. 7.
Equanimous action regarding pleasure, suffering, and that which is neither.
8. The karma of being without inferiority;
9. The karma of non-retrogression;
10. The karma of gathering skillful means.
11. The activity of aversion toward that which is to be remedied; one should know that this has two distinct phrases. 12.
The activity of uninterrupted mental attention (*manasikāra*).

13. The activity of superior progress; one should know that this has seven distinct phrases, namely: because of the correct application of the six *pāramitās*, and because of the correct application of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

14. The activity of fulfilling the practice (*paripūri-prayoga-karma*): one should know that this has six distinct points, namely: associating with virtuous friends; hearing the true Dharma; dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*); abandoning evil discursive thoughts; and the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*)—of which one should further know there are two distinct points; and the cultivation of the qualities of the associates (*sahāya-guṇa*)—of which one should further know there are two distinct points.

15. The activity of fulfillment (*pariniṣpatti-karma*): one should know that this has three distinct points, namely: immeasurable purity; attaining great majestic power (*mahānubhāva*); and the realization of spiritual qualities (*guṇa*).

Sixteenth, regarding the establishment of that karma, there are four points of distinction to be understood: namely, the virtue of governing the assembly; providing instruction and admonition with certainty and without doubt; gathering [disciples] through both material goods and the Dharma; and possessing a mind free from defilement.
It should be understood that all these phrases are variations of the first phrase.
As it is said:
"Because of the first phrase, there are distinct categories of qualities within the phrases."
"By virtue of the initial phrase, there is a distinction in meaning between the phrases.

Chapter Four: The Section on Entering the Characteristics of the Knowable (*Jñeyalakṣaṇapraveśa*) from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Thus, the characteristics of the knowable have already been explained. How should one view the "entry into the characteristics of the knowable"?
The basis for the cultivation of extensive learning is not subsumed under the *ālayavijñāna*, yet it functions as a seed in the same manner as the *ālayavijñāna*.

It consists of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) accompanied by a vision, which arises as something resembling phenomena and their meanings, appearing as if they were external objects of apprehension, and is subsumed under correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
In this regard, who is capable of entering into the characteristics of that which is to be known?

It is the bodhisattva whose mental continuum is permeated by extensive hearing of the Mahāyāna, who has already encountered and served immeasurable Buddhas appearing in the world, who has attained resolutely determined superior understanding (*adhimukti*), and who has well accumulated all roots of goodness, thereby being fully equipped with the provisions of merit and wisdom.
Where can one enter?

It is precisely within that mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) which appears as phenomena (*dharma*) and objects (*artha*), and which is produced by the signs (*nimitta*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna Dharma;

[this occurs] during the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the ultimate path (*niṣṭhā-mārga*). This is because, regarding all phenomena, one follows what has been heard and develops resolute belief in their nature as representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*); because one penetrates them according to reality; because one remedies all obstacles; and because one is free from all obstacles.
By what means can one enter?

It is by being sustained by the power of the roots of goodness; that is to say, by refining the mind through three modes, by abandoning four points, and by practicing with constant, earnest application toward the objects of the Dharma and its meaning through calm abiding and insight, without negligence.
In immeasurable world systems, immeasurable persons and sentient beings realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment moment by moment; this is the first way to temper one's mind.
By means of this intention, one is able to practice the perfections such as generosity;
having already attained such an intention, I shall, by virtue of it, achieve the fulfillment of the perfections such as generosity with little effort—this is the second exercise of the mind.

"If those who have accomplished wholesome qualities that are subject to obstacles are reborn with all their desired physical bases complete at the time of death, then since I possess sublime and unobstructed wholesome qualities, why should I not obtain every perfection at that time? This is called the third refinement of the mind.
In this regard, there is a verse:
“The sentient beings within the human realm Are infinite in number and location;
Since they realize equal enlightenment in every thought-moment, One ought not to feel discouraged.”
Those with pure mental dispositions are able to practice generosity and the like;
having attained this excellence, they are thus able to cultivate generosity and so forth.
When such virtuous ones face death, they attain the fulfillment of their own wishes according to their inclinations.
"How can supreme virtue, through its eternal abandonment, not be perfected?
This is because one abandons the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas by being free from them;
and because one removes doubt regarding the Mahāyāna by being able to eternally abandon the doubts of divergent wisdoms.
Because one abandons the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self regarding the phenomena that have been heard and contemplated, one severs attachment to phenomena;
because one is without volitional engagement or conceptual differentiation toward all manifest, present, and established signs, one severs conceptualization.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Abiding naturally in the manifest presence, Establishing all phenomena,
The wise do not engage in conceptual discrimination, And thus attain supreme enlightenment."
By what means and how does one gain entry?

One enters by means of mental verbalization—which, though appearing as phenomena and their objects, is comprised of appropriate attention of the type derived from the perfuming of hearing—and by means of the four investigations:
that is, the investigation of designations regarding names, objects, intrinsic natures, and distinctions.

Furthermore, it is by means of four kinds of thorough knowledge as-it-is (*yathābhūta-parijñā*), namely: thorough knowledge as-it-is regarding the designation of names, things, intrinsic natures, and distinctions; for all such [designations] are equally unapprehendable.

Because Bodhisattvas thus practice the preparatory application (*prayoga*) in accordance with reality in order to enter into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), they investigate the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that resembles words and resembles meanings, and find that words and names are merely mental verbalization; they investigate the meaning based upon these words and names and find it also to be merely mental verbalization; and they investigate the intrinsic nature and specific differences of names and meanings and find them to be merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

When one realizes that there is only mental discourse (*manojalpa*), at that time one realizes and knows that whether it be names, objects, intrinsic natures, or distinctions, all are merely provisional designations; because the characteristics of intrinsic nature and distinction do not exist as objective referents, they are equally unapprehendable.

By means of the four investigations and the four kinds of thorough knowledge as it truly is, one is able to penetrate this mental verbalization—which appears as words and appears as meaning—and realize that there is only the nature of consciousness.
In this realization of the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), what is realized?
How is it realized?
One realizes the nature of representation-only through the two natures of the grasped and the grasper, as well as their various aspects.
Because the six kinds of objects—namely, name, meaning, intrinsic nature, distinction, the conventional nature of intrinsic nature, and the conventional nature of distinction—are all non-existent;
because the nature of the grasped and the grasper manifests before one;
and because it arises simultaneously appearing as various kinds of signs and meanings.
It is like a rope appearing as a snake in the darkness; for example, the snake on the rope is not real because it does not exist.
If one has already understood that the object [the snake] is non-existent, then although the cognition of the snake ceases, the cognition of the rope remains.

If one analyzes it by way of subtle categories, this too is false, because its characteristics are color, odor, taste, and tangibility; thus, this cognition of a "rope" should be sublated by the cognition of its constituent parts.

In this way, when the unreal sixfold aspects of meaning are suppressed within those mental verbalizations that appear as words and meanings, the cognition of the nature of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā) must likewise be eliminated—just as the cognition of a snake is eliminated—by means of the cognition of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).

In this way, because the bodhisattva enters into the appearance of objects as they arise from mental verbalization, he enters into the nature of the thoroughly imagined; because he enters into consciousness-only, he enters into the nature of the dependent origination. How does he enter into the nature of the perfected reality?

When one has already eliminated the conceptualization of representation-only—which is of the nature of the habitual perfuming of hearing the Dharma through mental verbalization—at that time, the Bodhisattva has already dispatched the conceptualization of objects; since no semblance of an object can arise, even the semblance of representation-only cannot arise.
By this cause and condition, abiding in the designation of non-conceptuality regarding all objects, one then attains direct vision within the dharmadhātu and dwells in union with it.

At that time, the Bodhisattva has already brought forth the non-conceptual wisdom in which the object of cognition and the cognizing subject are equally equal; by virtue of this, the Bodhisattva is said to have realized and entered the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding this, there is a verse: “Phenomena, persons, phenomena, meaning, concise and extensive,
nature, impurity, purity, and the ultimate— these are the distinctions in the range of names.”
In this way, because the bodhisattva enters into the nature of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā), they enter into the characteristics of the objects of knowledge;

by entering into this, they enter the Stage of Utmost Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), thoroughly penetrate the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), are born into the family of the Tathāgatas, attain the mind-nature equal to all sentient beings, attain the mind-nature equal to all bodhisattvas, and attain the mind-nature equal to all Buddhas—this is called the bodhisattva’s path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Furthermore, for what purpose does one enter the nature of representation-only?

It is because of the supramundane wisdom of calm abiding and insight that takes all phenomena as its object, and because of the subsequently attained wisdom that recognizes the various marks of consciousness.

It is for the purpose of severing the seeds of the various characteristics of the ālayavijñāna; for the purpose of increasing the seeds capable of touching the dharmakāya; for the purpose of transforming the basis; for the desire to realize all Buddha-dharmas; and for the desire to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) by entering the nature of vijñaptimātratā.

Furthermore, through subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one perceives the nature of all representations (*vijñapti*) produced by the ālayavijñāna as being like an illusion and so forth, without error. Therefore, the bodhisattva is like a magician who, regarding the illusory objects, the various characteristics, and the teaching of cause and effect, is always free from inversion.

When entering into this realization of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), there are four kinds of meditative absorption (*samādhi*); these are the bases for the four stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
How should they be understood?

It should be understood that through the four investigations, within the stage of receptivity toward the inferior level of the non-existence of objects, there arises the samādhi of "attainment of clarity," which is the basis for the "heat" stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Within the superior stage of patience regarding the absence of external objects, there is the samādhi of increased clarity, which is the basis for the "summit" stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Furthermore, by means of the four kinds of thorough knowledge of reality as it is, one has entered into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and attained certainty regarding the absence of external objects; at this point, there is the samādhi of entering one portion of the true meaning, which is the basis for the "patience that accords with the truths" (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*).

Immediately following this, by subduing the notion of "representation-only" (vijñapti-mātra), there arises the "uninterrupted samādhi" (ānantarya-samādhi), which is the basis for the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma).
It should be understood that such samādhis belong to the stage of the "limits of clear realization" (abhisamaya-antya).

Thus, when a bodhisattva has already entered the stages (*bhūmi*), attained the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), and entered into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), how does one practice within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?

Within the framework of the ten stages as they have been established—which encompasses all sūtras appearing before one—one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) by means of the supramundane and subsequently attained wisdom of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) that takes the general dharma as its object, and by practicing this for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* eons.
One practices with diligent effort in order to realize the three bodies of a Buddha.
What is the difference between the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of a śrāvaka and the clear realization of a bodhisattva?
It should be understood that the clear realization of a bodhisattva differs from that of a śrāvaka by way of eleven kinds of distinctions:
First, by way of the distinction of the object of focus, because it takes the Mahāyāna teachings as its object of focus.
Second, by way of the distinction of the supporting provisions, because it takes the two types of provisions—great merit and great wisdom—as its supporting provisions.
Third, by way of the distinction of thorough penetration, because one is able to thoroughly penetrate the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Fourth, by way of the distinction of nirvāṇa, because one embraces the great non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-mahānirvāṇa*).
5. By way of the distinction of stages (*bhūmi*), because one attains deliverance by relying on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
6 and 7. By way of the distinction of purification, because one abandons the habitual tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*) and purifies the Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*).
8. Because of the distinction of attaining a mind of equality toward oneself and others, there is uninterrupted application in maturing sentient beings.
9. Because of the distinction of birth, one is born into the family of the Tathāgatas.
Tenth, by way of the distinction of birth, because one constantly takes birth within the great assemblies of all Buddhas.
Eleventh, by way of the distinction of fruition, because the fruits of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique buddha-qualities, and immeasurable merits are brought to full completion.
In this regard, there are two verses:
"Name and thing are mutual guests; Their nature should be investigated.
Regarding these two as well, one should analyze them As being merely measure and merely designation."
"True wisdom contemplates the absence of objects; there is only the threefold conceptualization.
Because that [object] does not exist, this [conceptualization] does not exist; this is precisely the entry into the three natures.
Furthermore, there are two verses of instruction as taught in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Treatise on the Analysis of Yoga):
"When the Bodhisattva abides in meditative equipoise, he observes that the reflected image is nothing but mind.
Once the characteristics of external objects have been eliminated, he scrutinizes that it is merely his own mental conception.
Thus dwelling within the internal mind, he knows that the apprehended object does not exist."
Next, the grasper is also non-existent; Finally, contact is found to be unobtainable.
Furthermore, there are five other verses on realization (*abhisamaya*), as taught in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*:
“The two provisions of merit and wisdom, The Bodhisattva has well prepared them without limit.”
Having thoroughly deliberated upon and correctly resolved the Dharma, one realizes that the meaning of objects is merely a category of words.
If one knows that all objects are but words, one then abides in the state of "mere mind" which resembles those objects;
thus, one is able to directly realize the true Dharmadhātu, whereby both dualistic appearances are completely eliminated.
Realizing through direct experience that there is no separate entity apart from the mind, one thereby understands that the mind itself does not exist.
The wise person, having thoroughly realized that both are non-existent, abides equally in the true dharma-realm where both are absent.
The wise possess the power of non-conceptual wisdom, Which acts universally, impartially, and in constant accordance with reality;
It extinguishes the thicket of dependencies and the mass of faults, Just as a great potent medicine neutralizes all poisons.

The Buddha has well-established the sublime Dharma; With wisdom and roots settled within the dharma-realm, One understands that the movement of thought is merely conceptual construction, And with heroic vigor, swiftly returns to the shore of virtue.

5. The Section on Entering Its Cause and Result (*Tad-avatāra-hetu-phala-vibhāga*). In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, the fifth section, "Entering Its Cause and Result": Having thus explained the entry into the characteristics of the knowable (*jñeya-lakṣaṇa-praveśa*), how is that entry into its cause and result to be understood?
That is to say, by means of the six perfections (pāramitās): generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
How does one enter into consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) by means of these six perfections?
Furthermore, how do the six *pāramitās* constitute the fruit of that entry?

It is said that when this bodhisattva does not cling to wealth or status, does not violate ethical discipline (*śīla*), remains unshaken by suffering, and is untiring in cultivation—such that these causes of distraction no longer manifest—the mind becomes one-pointed and is able to discern all phenomena according to reality, thereby entering into *vijñapti-mātra*.
Having entered into consciousness-only by relying on the six pāramitās, the bodhisattva realizes the six kinds of pāramitās that are subsumed within the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).

Therefore, even if one does not currently engage in the application of the six perfections, by virtue of gaining resolute faith (*adhimukti*) in the sacred teachings and through the mental engagements (*manasikāra*) of cherishing, rejoicing in, and delighting in them, one will constantly and uninterruptedly cultivate the six perfections through the method of meditative union, thereby swiftly attaining their fulfillment.
In this regard, there are three verses:
"Having perfected the white dharmas;
and having attained sharp and swift patience;"
Regarding the profound and vast teachings of their own vehicle, Bodhisattvas realize that all is mere conceptual construction; thus they attain non-conceptual wisdom.
Through the purity of their aspiration and conviction, their resolute intention becomes pure.
"In the past and within this stream of Dharma, All have been able to see the Buddhas;
They know that Bodhi is near, Because it is obtained without difficulty.
By these three verses, the seven aspects of the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) are collectively revealed:

That is to say, by way of the provisions (*sambhāra*), forbearance (*kṣānti*), the object of focus (*ālambana*), mental attention (*manasikāra*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the auspicious signs (*nimitta*), and the benefits (*anuśaṃsa*).
One should understand that these verses (*gāthā*) reveal [these topics] in their respective order.
For what reasons are there exactly six perfections?
Because they establish the remedies for the obstacles to be countered;
because they serve as the basis for realizing all Buddha-dharmas; and because they accord with the ripening of all sentient beings.
In order to counteract the causes for failing to set out [on the path], the perfections of generosity and ethical discipline are established.
The causes for failing to set out consist of attachment to wealth and status, as well as attachment to the household life.
The perfections of patience (*kṣānti*) and vigor (*vīrya*) are established as antidotes to the causes for retreating, even after one has already set out on the path.

These causes for retreating are: the manifold sufferings arising from the transgressions of sentient beings within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and the weariness produced by the prolonged application of oneself to virtuous qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*).
In order to counteract the causes of ruin—despite having already set out on the path so as not to regress—the perfections of meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā) are established.
The causes of ruin refer to all forms of mental distraction and erroneous wisdom.
Thus, because the antidotes and the obstacles they counteract are established in this way, only six numbers are established.
Furthermore, the first four perfections are the causes for non-distraction, while the subsequent one perfection is the accomplishment of non-distraction.
Because this non-distraction serves as the basis, one realizes the true meaning of all phenomena exactly as they are, and is thereby able to realize all Buddha-dharmas.
Since it is the locus upon which the realization of these Buddha-dharmas depends, only six [perfections] are established.
By means of the perfection of generosity, one is able to correctly gather in all sentient beings;
by means of the perfection of ethical discipline, one is able to refrain from harming sentient beings;
and by means of the perfection of patience, one is able to endure harm even when it is encountered.
By means of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), one is able to assist in the undertaking of what ought to be done.
Through such causes and conditions of gathering and benefiting others, sentient beings are rendered capable in the matter of maturation.

From this point onward, those whose minds are not yet stabilized shall attain stabilization; those whose minds are already stabilized shall attain liberation; and at the time of awakening, they shall reach maturity.
In this way, one should understand that the number six is established solely because it accords with the maturation of all sentient beings.
How are these six aspects to be perceived?
It is due to six kinds of preeminence:
first, preeminence of the basis, which means having the bodhicitta as its basis;
second, preeminence of the practice, which means being fully endowed with its actualization.
3. By way of the excellence of the basis (*āśraya*), meaning that it takes as its basis the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings;
4. By way of the excellence of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), meaning that it is embraced by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Fifth, by way of the excellence of dedication, meaning it is dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Sixth, by way of the excellence of purity, meaning it arises from being free from the obstructions of both the afflictive and cognitive hindrances.
Is that which is giving necessarily a pāramitā?
Or is that which is a pāramitā necessarily giving?
There are cases where there is giving that is not a pāramitā; thus, one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
Just as it is with generosity, so it should be understood that for each of the other perfections, one should likewise formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
For what reason are these six perfections taught in this specific order?
This means that each preceding pāramitā gives rise to the subsequent pāramitā in accordance with it.
Furthermore, how should one understand the etymological explanations (*nirukti*) of these various pāramitās?

Among all the roots of virtue, such as generosity, practiced by those in the world, by śrāvakas, and by pratyekabuddhas, these are the most excellent; because they can reach the further shore, they are collectively termed pāramitās.
Furthermore, because it can shatter stinginess and poverty, and can induce vast wealth, status, merit, and provisions, it is called "giving" (*dāna*);
because it can extinguish immoral conduct and miserable rebirths, and can attain fortunate rebirths and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "ethical discipline" (*śīla*);
and because it can utterly eliminate anger and enmity, and can cause oneself and others to dwell securely in peace, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, because it can distance one from all laziness and unwholesome dharmas, and can give rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas so that they increase, it is called diligence (*vīrya*);
because it can eliminate all distraction and induce the mind to abide in tranquility, it is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
and because it can dispel all dogmatic views and erroneous wisdom, and can truly and analytically discern phenomena, it is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
How should one understand the cultivation of these perfections?
It should be understood that this cultivation is, in brief, of five kinds:

first, cultivation through the application of manifest activity; second, cultivation through resolute conviction; third, cultivation through mental attention; fourth, cultivation through skillful means; and fifth, cultivation for the accomplishment of tasks.
Among these, the four types of cultivation have already been explained as before.

As for the cultivation of accomplishing activities, it refers to the effortless and uninterrupted performance of the Buddha-activities of all Tathāgatas, wherein they further practice the six pāramitās within their already perfected pāramitās.

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation through mental attention (*manasikāra*), it refers to the cultivation of six types of mental attention—namely, cherishing, sympathetic joy, and joyful aspiration—which are subsumed under six kinds of intentionality (*āśaya*):

first, the expansive intentionality; second, the long-term intentionality; third, the joyful intentionality; fourth, the gratitude-based intentionality; fifth, the great-vow intentionality; and sixth, the pure-intention intentionality.

If Bodhisattvas, even for as many countless great eons as it takes to manifest and realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, were to—at every single moment throughout that duration—suddenly renounce all their bodies and lives, and offer to the Tathāgatas worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filled with the seven treasures, continuing until they sit upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, such Bodhisattvas would still have no sense of satiety in their resolute intention for giving.

Throughout that duration, at every single moment—even if the trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire, and even if one were constantly deprived of all necessities of life during the four postures—the bodhisattva’s mind would constantly engage in ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), continuing until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Such a bodhisattva’s aspiration regarding ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom remains insatiable;
this is called the bodhisattva’s vast aspiration (*udāra-āśaya*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas maintain an insatiable intentionality toward this very [practice] until they sit upon the seat of sublime awakening, doing so constantly and without interruption, this is called the bodhisattva’s long-term intentionality.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings through the six perfections and thereby experience profound joy that cannot be matched by those sentient beings who receive the benefit, this is called the bodhisattva’s intentionality of joy.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings through the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), they perceive those beings as having rendered them great kindness and do not perceive themselves as having rendered kindness to them; this is called the bodhisattva’s intentionality of bearing gratitude.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas dedicate with a profound mind the roots of virtue accumulated through these six perfections to all sentient beings, so that they may attain desirable and superior fruits of maturation, this is called the bodhisattva’s great aspirational intention (*adhyāśaya*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas dedicate the roots of virtue accumulated through these six perfections (pāramitās) to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) for the sake of all sentient beings together with themselves, this is called the bodhisattva’s purely virtuous intention (āśaya).
In this way, a bodhisattva cultivates this attention of cherishing, which is subsumed by these six types of intentionality.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva deeply rejoices with a sincere mind in the immeasurable roots of goodness associated with the cultivation of the six types of intentionality by other bodhisattvas; thus, a bodhisattva cultivates this intentionality of rejoicing, which is subsumed by these six types of intentionality.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas, with their profound resolve, take great delight in the cultivation of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) as subsumed within the six types of aspiration for all sentient beings; they also vow that their own persons shall never be separated from this cultivation of the six perfections until they sit upon the seat of sublime enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). In this way, the bodhisattva cultivates the mental attention of delight as subsumed within these six types of aspiration.

If anyone, having heard this cultivation of mental attention subsumed under the six types of bodhisattva intention, should give rise to even a single thought of faith, they will still produce an immeasurable mass of merit and all their evil karmic obstructions will be extinguished; how much more so for a bodhisattva!
How are the distinctions among these pāramitās to be understood?
One should know that each has three categories.
Regarding the three categories of generosity: first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of material wealth; and third, the gift of fearlessness.

The three categories of ethical discipline (*śīla*) are: first, the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*); second, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*); and third, the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

The three categories of patience (*kṣānti*) are: first, the patience of enduring enmity and harm (*apakāra-marṣaṇa-kṣānti*); second, the patience of accepting suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*); and third, the patience of discerning the dharma (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*).

Regarding the three categories of diligence: first, armor-like diligence; second, diligence of application; and third, diligence that is without cowardice, without regression, and without complacency.
The three categories of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are: first, the meditative concentration of abiding; second, the meditative concentration of elicitation;

and third, the meditative concentration of accomplishing tasks. The three categories of wisdom (*prajñā*) are: first, non-conceptual preparatory wisdom; second, non-conceptual wisdom; and third, non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom.
How can such mutual inclusion be understood?
It is because this is able to include all wholesome dharmas, as it is their characteristic, as it accords with them, and as it is their outflow.
How are the various afflictions subsumed under these objects of abandonment to be understood?
They are to be seen as being of this nature, having this cause, and having this result.
How are the benefits obtained through these six perfections to be understood?

This refers to the fact that all bodhisattvas are encompassed by the cycle of birth and death through their possession of wealth and nobility; they are encompassed by noble birth; they are encompassed by being surrounded by a great circle of friends and a great retinue; they are encompassed by the accomplishment of the application of vast undertakings; they are encompassed by being free from afflictions and harm due to having naturally thin defilements; and they are encompassed by their skillful knowledge of all crafts, treatises, and fields of learning.

Supreme birth, freedom from fault, and even sitting upon the sublime seat of enlightenment while constantly manifesting all that is beneficial for the welfare of all sentient beings—this is called the benefit.
How are these six kinds of *pāramitā* to be understood as mutually determining one another?

In this regard, the Blessed One has, in some instances, spoken of all six *pāramitās* by means of the term "giving" (*dāna*); in some instances, by means of the term "ethical discipline" (*śīla*); in some instances, by means of the term "patience" (*kṣānti*); in some instances, by means of the term "diligence" (*vīrya*); in some instances, by means of the term "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*); and in some instances, by means of the term "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
What is the intended meaning of what has been stated?
It means that within the cultivation of the application of any one *pāramitā*, all *pāramitās* mutually assist and bring it to completion; such is the intended meaning.
In this regard, there is a summary verse (uddāna):
"Number, characteristics, and sequence; etymological definition, cultivation, and differentiation;
inclusion, the counteracted, and qualities—these should be understood as mutual determinations."
